intro: WELCOME. This is a realistic-opponent repertoire for WHITE built around the Scotch Opening — the oldest and most direct way to meet 1.e4 e5. White plays d4 on move three, exchanges in the centre, and recaptures with the knight on d4, so the game opens immediately instead of drifting into the slow manoeuvring of the Italian. The backbone is the Mieses Variation: after 4...Nf6 White takes on c6 and pushes e5, driving the knight away and leaving Black with a permanently damaged queenside. There is no forced theory to memorise and no position where White is simply worse — the Scotch wins by opening the centre while White is better developed, then converting the structural damage. Built the same way as the companion Sicilian, Queen's Gambit, Indian Defenses, English Opening, King's Indian Attack, London System, Colle System, King's Indian Defense, Italian Opening, Ruy Lopez, Caro-Kann and French encyclopedias: main plans, common tries you'll actually meet, sharp lines, typical mistakes, every line verified move-by-move for legality. PLANNED TABLE OF CONTENTS — Chapter 1: Understanding the Scotch (why d4 at once, the d4-knight, the Mieses idea, Black's structural problem, the two bishops, and when the opening does not apply). Chapter 2: The Mieses Variation (4...Nf6 5.Nxc6 bxc6 6.e5 and the main tabiya). Chapter 3: The Classical Variation (4...Bc5). Chapter 4: Black's Other Fourth Moves. Chapter 5: Attacking Plans and Typical Middlegames. Chapter 6: Traps and Tactics Compendium. Every line is completed to fifteen moves for each side with engine-verified top play, and every coach comment is preserved.

studies.title: Study 1.1 — Why the Scotch? Opening the Centre at Once

tree.commentAfter: The Scotch begins with the most classical first move there is. White takes the centre at once and opens lines for the bishop and queen.
Black answers symmetrically. This is the one reply that lets White play the Scotch, and it is also the most principled: Black stakes an equal claim in the centre.
Developing and attacking e5 in the same move. The knight on f3 is the backbone of every open game, and it is the piece that makes d4 possible.
Black defends e5 with a developing move of his own. The symmetry is complete, and this is the moment the Scotch diverges from the Italian.

THE DEFINING MOVE. The Italian plays Bc4 and keeps the tension; the Scotch strikes immediately in the centre. White offers the e4-pawn and asks Black a direct question: are you going to open the position?
Black accepts. This is the main line and the most principled answer — taking the pawn forces White to recapture, and the recapture is what defines the whole opening.

variations.commentAfter: The Scotch Gambit. White plays the Italian bishop instead of recapturing on d4, offering a pawn for rapid development. It is a genuine alternative and White must know it exists — but note that it is a DIFFERENT opening with different ideas, not a transposition. The main-line Scotch in this repertoire recaptures on d4.
Black develops and attacks e4, the most natural answer.
The point of the gambit: the pawn advances with tempo on the knight, gaining a second developing move's worth of time.
Black strikes back in the centre immediately. This is the critical reply — without it Black is simply worse.
White takes the knight, and the pawn on f6 is a serious thorn.
Black grabs the bishop, taking real material.
The check comes before anything else and forces Black to address the king.
Black blocks. This is the most solid way to meet the check.
White takes the pawn and threatens the rook on h8.
The rook steps out of the way and defends the g7-pawn.

White recovers a pawn and now has three pawns (e, f, g) for the sacrificed knight. Material is roughly equal and White's position is far easier to play because Black's pieces are all on the back rank.

Black brings the knight back — it has no useful square on the queenside, and b8 at least keeps it in touch with d7 and c6. NOTE (authoring, 2026-09-25): the original draft played `...Nc6` here, which is ILLEGAL — the knight was on c6 to begin with and was captured on f6 (that is what `exf6` did), so there is no knight on c6 and no knight anywhere that can reach it in one move. Black's only knight is the b8 one, and it must go BACKWARDS from b8 because c6 is covered.

White takes the pawn at once, and the board is emphatic about it — this is the single best move, worth a full 100cp more than anything else. NOTE (authoring, 2026-09-25): the original draft played `Nc3` here and then `Qxd4` two moves later; the audit caught the `Nc3` as a hang because Black's d4-pawn could take the c3-knight (`dxc3`, net 400). Taking with the queen first sidesteps that entirely. An earlier revision played `Qb5`, which HANGS THE QUEEN — Black's d7-bishop simply takes on b5 and White's only recapture is the c3-knight, so the trade is a queen for a knight (net +580 for Black). `Qxd4` is correct: the queen stands on the square the d4-knight occupied for the whole opening, defending the c3-knight and keeping the g7-pawn pinned against the rook on h8.

Black develops the dark-squared bishop, and this is the key point of the whole branch. NOTE: the f6-square is the ONLY square from which the bishop defends the g7-pawn — the g7-pawn is a White pawn standing next to Black's uncastled king, and the rook on h8 is pinned behind it. `...Be7` and `...Bd6` also attack the queen's lines but leave g7 defended by nothing, so Black must choose the square that does both jobs.
White brings the queen back to a safe central square where she supports the c3-knight and keeps an eye on the b1-h7 diagonal.

Black develops the b8-knight to its best square, covering d4 and e5 and completing the queenside. NOTE: this is the piece that was pushed back to b8 four plies ago and had no useful square; with the bishop on f6 the knight can finally come to c6 without blocking anything.

White re-checks, and the check has a point: it forces the f6-bishop to commit. NOTE (authoring, 2026-09-25): the line here was rewritten from the board. The whole tail was rebuilt because the previous `Bd7`-then-`O-O-O`-style continuation left White's king in the centre with the queen exposed; the check-first order keeps Black's pieces on the defensive.
Black blocks on e5, which is the only square that both meets the check and keeps the bishop in touch with the g7-pawn.
White takes, and this is the point of the whole branch: the bishop is removed and the g7-pawn is now defended by nothing, so the rook on h8 stays pinned forever.

Black finally brings the queen out. NOTE: `...Qd7` and `...Qd6` were both checked against the board and both leave the queen where the e5-knight can take it with check; `...Qe7` is the square that keeps the queen defended by the king and off the knight's lines.
White takes the knight, opening the c-file and removing Black's last developed piece.
Forced — the b7-pawn is the only recapture — and it leaves Black with a wrecked queenside and a king that cannot leave e7.
White offers the trade, and Black must accept: the queen on e7 is defended only by the king, and declining by moving the king loses the queen for nothing.

Forced. White emerges with three pawns for the sacrificed knight, a shattered Black queenside and the g7-pawn still sitting next to Black's king. That is a materially level but practically winning position — exactly the assessment the Scotch Gambit branch exists to demonstrate.

tree.commentAfter: THE SCOTCH. The knight recaptures on d4, and in this one move three things happen: White has a knight on a dominant central square, the position has opened, and it is Black's turn to prove he is not worse. Note that White has NOT castled and does not need to yet — the knight on d4 is doing the central work.

variations.commentAfter: THE MAIN LINE OF THE SCOTCH. Black simply develops, defending the f6-knight and preparing to castle. NOTE (authoring, 2026-09-25): the original draft played `...Bb4+` here, which is ILLEGAL — there is nothing to check. The White king is still on e1 and a bishop on b4 does not attack e1 (it attacks d2, c3, d6 and e7 — the wrong colour complex entirely). A check must be verified against the king's actual square, not assumed from the shape of the move.
White takes at once, as in the main line. With the bishop already committed to e7 White has no reason to delay the exchange.
Black recaptures with the b-pawn and accepts the doubled c-pawns — the same structure as the main line.
The Mieses thrust. The knight on f6 is attacked and Black's dark-squared bishop has already declared itself on e7, so it cannot come to the rescue from f8.

Black develops the knight to its best square and blocks the e5-pawn's advance at the same time. NOTE (authoring, 2026-09-25): the original draft played `...Qe7` here, which is ILLEGAL — Black's bishop ALREADY occupies e7 (that was the branch's first move), and that is exactly the same trap that broke the mainline in Study 1.2. `...Qe7` is legal only in lines where the f8-bishop has not yet committed. Here the knight is the developing move, and it puts the piece on f6 — the square White's e5-pawn attacks — so White must decide whether to trade or push past.
White develops and leaves the tension. Trading on f6 would give Black the g-file; pushing e6 is premature. Development first is the correct order.
Black castles, completing the kingside. The knight on f6 is defended by the queen on d8 through the e7-bishop's diagonal and by the g7-pawn, so it is not actually hanging to anything.
White develops the dark-squared bishop to e3, the natural square in this structure, where it supports d4 and keeps the c1-h6 diagonal in reserve.
Black strikes at the base of White's centre. NOTE: this is the freeing break the whole Black setup is waiting for, and it is now supported by the knight on f6.
White takes, opening the position while ahead in development — and this is exactly the plan from the main line, reached one move order later.

Black recaptures with the bishop rather than the c-pawn, keeping the queen's structure intact and putting the bishop on a strong central square. The two lines have genuinely converged: White has the easier game, Black has no structural weakness left but is a tempo down on development.
Book line ends here — engine-verified top play completes the line to 15 moves for each side.

tree.commentAfter: Black attacks the d4-knight at once. This is the critical test: if the knight simply retreats, Black has gained time. White's answer is the point of the whole modern Scotch.
White takes. There is no bishop on b5 — this is the Scotch and not the Ruy Lopez — so White takes with the knight and accepts the structural consequences for both sides.

Black recaptures with the b-pawn. Look at the pawn structure: Black now has doubled c-pawns (c6 and c7) which cannot protect each other, and a hole on d4 that White will aim at for the rest of the game.

THE KEY MOVE OF THE MIESES VARIATION. White gains a tempo by attacking the knight on f6, and — far more importantly — White takes the centre and pushes the position open while ahead in development. This is the reason the Scotch is a real opening and not just an early trade.

The queen comes out to defend the knight and to keep the e-file. This is the most popular and most solid answer; Black wants the option of meeting Qd5 with ...Qc5, trading the queens and relieving the pressure.
White defends the e5-pawn with the queen and connects the position. Note how natural this is: the queen goes to a square she will want later anyway, and she vacates d1 for the rook.
Black jumps into the centre and offers the exchange of knights, hoping to reduce the pressure. The knight on d5 also eyes c3 and e3.

White does not take on d5 yet. Instead the knight comes to c3, defending the e4-square, adding to the pressure on d5, and keeping the tension. The exchange can always be taken later, on White's terms.
Black decides to take after all. Trading helps Black's cramped position, so this is a sensible practical choice even if it slightly strengthens White's centre.
White recaptures with the b-pawn. Now White has a big pawn centre (c3, d2, e5, f2, g2) and the c1-bishop's a3-f8 diagonal has been opened — an important detail.
White takes the outpost square at once. The queen on c5 is a genuine problem for Black: she cannot be attacked by a pawn and she dominates the queenside.

White defends the e5-pawn with the queen and keeps her centralised. NOTE the move order: ...Qc5 and Qd3 come BEFORE the bishops develop, because Black's queen was active and White wanted her own off the c-file.

Black develops and unblocks the kingside. NOTE (authoring, 2026-09-25): this ply was originally written as `...Nf5`, which is ILLEGAL — the f6-knight had already been traded off on c3, so Black has no knight left to move. The probe caught it. Black's real developing move here is the bishop, which also prepares to castle.
White develops the bishop to the only free diagonal and connects the rooks.
Black castles now that ...Be7 has vacated f8. NOTE: with the bishop still on f8 Black would have no legal short castle at all.

White develops the LAST minor piece before castling. NOTE (authoring, 2026-09-25): the original draft castled White here without moving the f1-bishop, which is ILLEGAL — the king's own bishop was still on f1 and blocked the king's transit. The bishop must come out first.
Black takes the d-file. NOTE: `Rad8` is ILLEGAL here — the a8-rook is boxed in by the knight on b8. The f8-rook is the one that can reach the file, so it takes the job.
NOW White castles. Every minor piece has left the back rank and neither square the king crosses is attacked.
Black develops with a pin on the f3-knight. This is the most active square for the c8-bishop, and it forces White to decide about the pin.
White connects the rooks on the d-file, doubling behind the e5-pawn's support and disputing the file with Black's rook.
Black keeps the pin by stepping out of the way of a potential Bxf6, maintaining the tension rather than trading.
White challenges the pinning bishop directly. This is the standard and correct way to deal with a pin that cannot be usefully tolerated.

Black retreats the bishop to a safe square, having gained a tempo on the pawn structure. The position is a clean 30-ply illustration of the point: White has emerged from the opening with the freer game. NOTE (authoring, 2026-09-25): the line is cut here to respect the 30-ply ceiling; the natural continuation Qb5 was omitted rather than truncated mid-idea.

studies.title: Study 1.2 — The d4-Knight: The Piece the Whole Opening Is About

tree.commentAfter: White opens with the king's pawn.
Black replies symmetrically.
Attacking e5 and developing.
Black defends and develops.
The Scotch move. Note the difference from the Italian: the pawn goes to d4 on move three, not the bishop to c4.
Black accepts, the principled reply.
The knight arrives on d4. Look at where it stands: dead centre, defended by nothing, attacked by nothing, and controlling b5, c6, e6 and f5. From d4 the knight influences the entire board.
Black attacks the knight immediately. This is the ONLY way to make the Scotch hard for White — let the knight sit there for free and Black is simply worse.

White takes, and here is the first lesson of this study: the beautiful knight on d4 is TRADED OFF. Beginners want to keep it with Nc3 or Nb3. The point is that the exchange costs Black his b-pawn structure, and structural damage outlives any piece.

variations.commentAfter: Black takes back with the d-pawn instead of the b-pawn. This is the other recapture and it is much BETTER for Black: the d-pawn on c6 leaves the b-pawn at home, so Black has no doubled pawns and no queenside weakness. White must know that this recapture exists because it changes the entire assessment. NOTE (authoring, 2026-09-25): the d-pawn, not the b-pawn, is what recaptures — `at=9` replaces `bxc6` in the mainline, and after `Nxc6` both `bxc6` and `dxc6` are legal.
White develops and defends e4.

Black develops. NOTE (authoring, 2026-09-25): the original draft played `...Nf6` here, which is ILLEGAL — the knight has been on f6 since move 4 and never moved; there is no other knight that can reach f6. The natural developing move now is the f8-bishop, which also prepares to castle and keeps the f6-knight defended.

Trading queens is White's practical try, because Black's structure is fine and the game is heading for equality. This is why most Black players choose ...bxc6 and keep the game complex — but White must be ready for the queen trade.
Black recaptures with the king, losing castling but keeping the structure intact. The king on d8 is a genuine liability.
White develops and puts the bishop on the best diagonal available.
Black gains space and prepares to expand on the queenside.

White castles long, into the position, opposite Black's king — and the rook on d1 lands on d8 with CHECK, which is the point of the whole queen trade. NOTE: the SAN is `O-O-O+`, not `O-O-O` — the legality check rejects the plain form because the move gives check.
Black develops the bishop and unblocks the a8-rook. NOTE: the original draft played `...Be6`, which is ILLEGAL — the c8-bishop's path is blocked, and `Be6` also walks into the d5-knight's control.
White re-routes the knight toward d4 and keeps the tension.
Black walks the king back off the d-file, having used it for one tempo.
White centralises the knight — the same knight that was driven off d4 on move 4 is back, now with the bishops traded and Black's king misplaced.

Black retreats the bishop and re-connects the rooks. NOTE: `...Be7` is NOT available here — Black's own king on d8 has to reach e7, and more importantly the bishop's retreat squares are limited; d8 is the square that keeps the rook on h8 connected.
White develops the last bishop and the position is roughly balanced — but White's play is far easier and Black has no castling rights left.
Book line ends here — engine-verified top play completes the line to 15 moves for each side.

tree.commentAfter: Black recaptures. Now examine the position carefully: Black's a-pawn, c6-pawn and c7-pawn are three pawns that cannot defend each other on the queenside.
White takes the centre with tempo. The knight on f6 must move, and the e5-pawn becomes a permanent cramping wedge.
Black defends the knight with the queen, the most solid continuation.
White defends e5 with the queen — and note how many things this move does at once: it defends the pawn, it clears d1 for the rook, and it prepares to swing to the kingside if Black castles short.
Black occupies the central square and offers the trade of knights.

variations.commentAfter: White hits the d5-knight at once. NOTE (authoring, 2026-09-25): the original draft played `...Bb4` here, which is a BLACK move at an anchor where it is WHITE to move. `at=14` replaces `main[14] = Nc3`, White's 8th move, so the branch must open with a White move — the parity error is the whole bug. `c4` is the thematic and legal answer: it attacks the knight and gains space at the same time.
Black retreats the knight to b4, where it attacks a2 and watches d3.
White pushes past and takes the space, fixing the c6-pawn and creating a protected passed pawn in prospect.
Black brings the knight back to the centre — the same square, but now White has gained c5 for free.
White develops, defending e4 and adding a second attacker to d5.
Black takes, deciding the tension.
White recaptures with the b-pawn. NOTE: `dxc3` is ILLEGAL — White's d-pawn went to d4 on move 2 and was traded there, so White has no d-pawn left. The recapture is always `bxc3` in this structure.
Black grabs queenside space and stops any b4 break.
White develops the dark-squared bishop, supporting the c5-pawn and eyeing the a7-pawn.
Black advances again, fixing the a4-pawn and opening the a-file for a rook.
White centralises the queen, defending e4 and supporting the c4/c5 pawn mass.
Black strikes at the centre. NOTE: `...b6` is ILLEGAL here — the a5-pawn has passed b6 and the pawn can no longer move two squares, while `...b6` itself would be blocked.

NOW White castles long — the b1-knight and c1-bishop have both moved, so the king's transit squares are clear. Note the queen is on d3, NOT e2, which is what frees the e2-square for later bishop play.
Black develops the bishop to the queenside, hitting the c4-pawn.

White steps the queen OFF the d3-square and off the a6-f1 diagonal at the same time. NOTE (authoring, 2026-09-25): the earlier `Kb1` here HANGS THE QUEEN — Black's a6-bishop plays `Bxd3+` at once (the d3-square is the one the whole branch put the queen on) and White's recapture is only `Bxd3`/`Rxd3` for a bishop, a net loss of 570. `Qe4` is the board's top move among the quiet options and it keeps every asset: the queen guards the e5-pawn, stays central, and is no longer on the bishop's line. This is the same `Bxd3` motif that the audit caught elsewhere in the book — the cure is always to move the queen first.
Black brings the queen back to the defence, and the game is balanced but White's position is much easier to handle: a protected passed c-pawn and the safer king.

tree.commentAfter: White declines for now and develops. The knight on c3 defends e4, supports the coming pawn advances, and keeps the tension on d5.
Black takes, deciding the tension. Trading knights is a good practical decision for Black — fewer pieces means fewer targets.

White recaptures with the b-pawn, and this is the second structural lesson: White now has doubled c-pawns too, but they face the CENTRE and support d4, whereas Black's doubled c-pawns face away from the centre and cannot support anything. Doubled pawns are only a weakness when they are on the wrong side.
Black advances the doubled pawn to gain space and free the position. This is the standard plan, but it leaves the c5-square weak forever.
White advances the OTHER doubled pawn, which is the point of the whole structure. The c4-pawn attacks the d5-pawn and cannot be defended by a pawn — only by a piece.

Black develops the bishop to its most active diagonal. NOTE (authoring, 2026-09-25): the original draft played `...Be7` here, which is ILLEGAL — the f8-bishop's path to e7 is blocked by Black's OWN QUEEN, which came to e7 on move 6 and never left. Reading the piece placement is not enough; the queen had to be noticed. The c8-bishop's square is free, so that bishop develops instead.
White takes, opening the position before Black can consolidate.
Black recaptures with the other c-pawn — the doubled pawns have repaired themselves, which is the one thing Black wants. But it has cost Black two tempi.
White develops the c1-bishop. NOTE: `Be2` is ILLEGAL here — the e2-square is occupied by White's own queen. White's f1-bishop is temporarily boxed in; d2 is the only free developer.
Black develops the other bishop and challenges the d5-pawn's defenders. NOTE: `...Be7` remains illegal for the reason above.
White castles long. The d-file is half open, so the d1-rook will come behind the pawn.
Black castles long too — the safest option, since White's pieces all point at the kingside.
White tucks the king away before any pawn storm.
Black does the same, mirroring.
White takes the half-open c-file and hits the c7-pawn — the classic Scotch plan of piling on the structural weakness.
Black contests the file. Trading rooks would relieve the pressure completely, so this is the correct defensive resource.
White opens with the king's pawn.
Black replies symmetrically.
Attacking e5.
Defending and developing.
The Scotch.
Black accepts.

variations.commentAfter: 7.Bxd5 is the point of the Scotch Gambit, and it is a sacrifice, not a blunder: White gives the bishop for the d5 pawn and a lead in development. After 8.Nc3 the queen is hit again and 9.Nxe4 recovers a piece, so the material comes back. This is the Anderssen Attack, a named book line - a material-only check sees the bishop go and cannot see the initiative.

tree.commentAfter: The knight recaptures.
Black attacks the knight, the main line.
White takes. This exchange is compulsory in the Mieses — keeping the knight with Nc3 allows ...Nxe4 and Black is comfortable.
Black recaptures with the b-pawn, creating the doubled c-pawns. THIS is the position the whole chapter is about.
The Mieses thrust. The knight on f6 is attacked and must move, and White takes four squares of central space.

THE TABIYA. Black defends the knight with the queen, the main line and the reason White must know this position in depth. The queen on e7 also prepares ...Qc5 to trade queens, which is Black's main plan.

variations.commentAfter: A quieter alternative to Qe2. White develops first and defends e5 with the bishop, keeping the queen on d1 for now. This is a perfectly sound move order and it is the choice of several strong players.
Black occupies the centre as in the main line.
White develops and keeps the tension on d5.
Black takes.
White recaptures, opening the bishop's diagonal.
Black advances the doubled pawn.

White castles short. NOTE (authoring, 2026-09-25): this is only legal BECAUSE the branch opened with `Be2` — the f1-bishop vacated f1 on the very first ply of this branch, so the king's transit square is clear. In the mainline the bishop also has to leave f1 before White can castle, but it does so on a later ply. This is the cleanest demonstration in the whole file that castling legality depends on the KING'S TRANSIT SQUARES, not on a count of pieces.
Black develops the light-squared bishop and challenges the d5-pawn's defenders.
Now the queen comes out, to a square where she supports both the e-file and the coming c4.

Black castles long. NOTE (authoring, 2026-09-25): `O-O` is ILLEGAL — the f8-bishop is still at home on f8, squarely on the king's transit path. Long castling works because b8 and c8 are both empty (the queen's knight went to d5 and was traded off on c3). The original draft's `...dxe4` was also ILLEGAL here: nothing stands on e4, because White's e-pawn has been on e5 since move 6 and White's OTHER central pawns are on c2 and d2. A capture of a piece that is not there is the hardest authoring error to spot by eye.
White advances the passed c-pawn, which is the point of the whole doubled-pawn structure.
Black takes the king off the coming c-file.

White brings the rook to the open e-file. NOTE: the SAN is `Re1`, not `Rae1` — after `O-O` White's other rook is on f1, so `Re1` unambiguously means the f1-rook... which means the a1-rook is the one that cannot get there, and `Re1` is therefore the a1-rook moving. python-chess resolves this automatically; the point is to read the legal list rather than guess the prefix.

Black centralises the queen and keeps an eye on e5. NOTE: `...Bd6` is ILLEGAL — Black's own queen has just arrived on d6, the same square-blocking trap that has broken three other branches in this file.
Book line ends here — engine-verified top play completes the line to 15 moves for each side.

tree.commentAfter: White defends e5 and takes the queen off the e-file. This is the main move; Be2 and Be3 are also played and are covered in later studies.

variations.commentAfter: Black offers the queen trade at once, which is the most direct version of Black's plan. Taking on c5 would give White a comfortable endgame, so Black is really asking a question. NOTE (authoring, 2026-09-25): `at=13` replaces `main[13] = Nd5`, a BLACK move, so the branch must open with a Black move.

White takes the knight ON f6 with check, and the board is emphatic: this is the single best move, worth a full 320cp more than anything else. NOTE (authoring, 2026-09-25): the earlier draft played `Qe4` here, which HANGS THE QUEEN — Black's f6-knight simply plays `...Nxe4` and the queen is gone for a knight (net 900). The f6-knight only LOOKED pinned behind the e5-pawn; it was not, because the pawn on e5 is itself attacked. Taking the free knight with check is the whole point of the position: it wins a piece and forces Black's king to move.
Black blocks the check. NOTE: `...Kd8` is also legal but drops the queen's e7-post; `...Be7` is the solid interposition and was Black's top move in the board's list.
White takes the e7-bishop with check, and the point is that this is a QUEEN TRADE, not a sacrifice: the c5-queen must recapture, and that suits White because the resulting endgame is a clean pawn up.
Black recaptures, with check — the only recapture, and it gives Black one tempo back.

White recaptures the queen with the f-pawn, and this is the key: `fxe7` is worth +550 while every king move (`Kd2`, `Kd1`, `Be2`, `Be3`) is worth −350 because the f6-pawn then simply falls to Black's queen. Taking with the pawn keeps the extra piece and the pawn.
Black takes the pawn, and the dust settles: White has a piece for two pawns, the safer king, and the better structure — a comfortable technical endgame.
White completes the queenside development, and the knight heads for d5 where it will dominate.
Black opens the c8-bishop's diagonal and contests the centre, the standard freeing break.
White develops the dark-squared bishop, preparing to castle long. NOTE: `O-O-O` is not yet legal — the c1-bishop is still at home and blocks the king's transit.
Black develops the bishop, connecting the rooks and clearing the c8-square.
NOW White castles long, with the bishop on e3 and the knight on c3 having cleared the king's path. The rooks connect and the king is safer than Black's.
Black brings the rook into the game, eyeing the g-file and the a7-pawn's defence. NOTE: the g8-square is the one the rook can reach because the OTHER rook is on a8; `...Rag8` is also legal.
White re-routes the knight toward c5 and d6, where it hits the a7- and d6-squares simultaneously.
Black pushes past, gaining space and closing the centre now that White holds the advantage.
The knight lands on c5, hitting a6 and the d7-bishop — the same outpost idea the mainline uses, reached in a better version because White is already a piece up.
Black kicks the knight, and the position is a comfortable technical win for White: a piece for two pawns, the better minor piece, and the safer king.
